videos.description:
Laura Lynne Jackson talks to people on the other side for a living. What she learned there changed how she sees death and grief.

In this episode, Laura Lynne Jackson and Jay Shetty talk about what a medium knows about death, and why she believes the people we love still reach us. Laura explains the difference between a psychic and a medium, the day at age 11 when she knew she had to go see her grandfather, and what scientists found when they put EEG scanners on her brain.

She shares the signs she says our loved ones send, from flickering lights to coins in our path, why she asks for aardvarks instead of butterflies, and a near-death study about a red shoe on the roof of a hospital.

Learn why a relationship with someone who died can grow stronger. And learn what a sign means when you are not sure it is real.

videos.title: The Confidence Trap, Explained
videos.description:
Back in the '70s there was a woman who couldn't wear a necklace. The weight of it on her collarbone reminded her of a snake, and she'd spent her entire adult life dodging snakes.

Then she had one afternoon with Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura. By the time she left, she had a snake in her lap.

OK, phobia cured. That's not the interesting part.

Bandura checked back in six months later. The fear was gone. But his participants were also speaking up at work. Asking for raises. Having fights they'd put off for years. Sticking to diets they'd quit.

And the necklace lady? Wearing necklaces.

They walked out of that room with one new fact about themselves, and it started poking holes in other limits they'd assumed were permanent.

Bandura built his most influential paper on it. Whether you'll take on something hard has very little to do with how you feel about yourself. It comes down to whether you've got evidence you can pull it off.

So what's your snake? Pick a piece of it small enough to do this week, nerves and all. Then see what else starts to budge.

videos.title: Why Cutting Off Family Is a Modern Option
videos.description:
For most of human history, cutting off your family wasn't much of an option. Your family was your job, your safety net and your retirement plan. If you left, you were on your own in a very literal way.

That's changed. You find work through LinkedIn instead of on your dad's farm. You can rent an apartment across the country, build a friend group from scratch, and never need a relative to vouch for you.

When survival no longer depends on family, the relationship has to stand on something else. For a lot of people, that's when they find out how much was holding it together.
